item.content:encoded:
Hello BNers,

Omotunde here.

From exploring futuristic smart homes and AI-powered manufacturing facilities to tasting Korean street food, discovering Seoul, and experiencing the country’s rich culture, my 5-day South Korea adventure with LG Electronics was unforgettable.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija)

Some trips leave you with beautiful photographs, others with unforgettable memories, and some leave you with a whole new perspective. My experience in South Korea with LG Electronics was a combination of all three.

South Korea had been on my travel wish list for a while, so finally getting the opportunity to visit was exciting in itself. But this was more than just a trip to a new destination. It was an opportunity to explore the world of LG Electronics, understand its journey, experience its innovations firsthand and discover how technology continues to shape the way we live.

Over five days, we explored different locations, met incredible people, exchanged ideas, experienced some of Korea’s most exciting innovations and, of course, made time to enjoy the country’s food, culture and lifestyle.

From Seoul to Changwon, every day brought something new.

Here’s a look at how the experience unfolded.

PART ONE: THE LG INNOVATION TOUR

Our LG experience began with an introduction to the company’s vision, its Home Appliance Solutions business, and its ambition to become a Smart Life Solution Company.

While many of us know LG for its home appliances, televisions, and consumer electronics, the tour offered a much broader understanding of the brand and the thinking behind its innovations.

At the LG Twin Towers, we were introduced to different aspects of the company’s business and got to explore some of its products and technologies, including the LG WashTower, InstaView refrigerator, Heat Pump Washer Dryer Combo, SolarDOM, and SKS premium appliances.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija)

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija)

What stood out to me was how much attention is being given to making everyday living smarter, more convenient, and more connected. It was interesting to see how products that perform familiar household functions are evolving through technology to offer entirely new experiences.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija)


It was a great introduction to what would become five days of learning and discovery.

Changwon Smart Park: Where AI, Robotics and Manufacturing Meet

One of the most insightful experiences of the tour was visiting LG Smart Park in Changwon.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija)

Before this visit, my idea of a manufacturing facility was largely shaped by traditional production lines and machinery. However, what I encountered at Changwon offered a completely different perspective.

From the Heritage Lounge, where we got an introduction to LG’s manufacturing journey, to the Lighthouse Factory experience, there was so much to learn about how the company is integrating artificial intelligence, robotics, data and automation into its manufacturing processes.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija)


Recognised by the World Economic Forum as a Lighthouse Factory, LG Smart Park demonstrates how advanced technologies can transform manufacturing and improve efficiency.

Seeing how robots, intelligent systems and people work together was particularly fascinating. It also got me thinking about the ongoing conversations around artificial intelligence and the future of work.

Rather than simply viewing AI as a technology that replaces human effort, I got to see how it can support people, take on repetitive tasks and improve the way complex processes are managed.

It was one of those visits that makes you appreciate just how much goes on behind the products we use every day.

LG Science Park: A Glimpse Into the Future

Our next stop was LG Science Park in Magok, Seoul, one of the company’s major research and development hubs.

This was another opportunity to see how LG is thinking about the future of technology and everyday living.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija)

We explored the LG AI Home experience, ThinQ Real Home, the Innovation Showroom and the D5 flagship experience.

The demonstrations offered a glimpse into what connected living could look like, with smart technologies and appliances working together to create a more seamless home experience.

Imagine a home where your appliances communicate with one another, respond intelligently to your needs and make everyday routines easier. That was the kind of future these experiences brought to life.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija)

It was fascinating seeing how research, technology and innovation are being translated into solutions that could eventually become part of our everyday lives.

And just when I thought there was already so much to take in, I got to meet CLOiD!

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija)


Meeting CLOiD: When the Future Becomes Real

Meeting a live robot called CLOiD was definitely one of those surreal moments of the trip.

We have seen robots in movies and watched countless videos of artificial intelligence and robotics, but seeing one up close and experiencing it in person is something else entirely.

It was fascinating to see how far robotics has come and how these technologies are moving beyond futuristic concepts into real-world applications.

Experiences like this make you pause and think about how different our everyday lives could look in the years ahead.

From Goldstar to LG: Understanding the Evolution of a Global Brand

Another interesting part of the tour was learning more about LG’s history and evolution.

The company’s story dates back to 1947, when it began as Lak Hui Chemical. In 1958, Goldstar was established, marking its entry into the electronics industry. The company eventually adopted the LG identity in 1995.

Getting to see this journey represented through its history, milestones and innovations gave me a deeper appreciation of how the brand has evolved over the decades.

It was particularly interesting learning about some of LG’s early milestones, including its first electric fan in 1960, refrigerator in 1965, air conditioner in 1968 and washing machine in 1969.

From those early innovations to the smart appliances and technologies we explored during the tour, it was a remarkable reminder of how far the company has come.

It also reinforced something I took away from the experience: innovation is not a one-time achievement. It requires continuous learning, improvement and the willingness to imagine what is possible beyond the present.

The LG Flagship Store: Experiencing Innovation in One Space

Our visit to the LG Flagship Store was a lovely way to bring different aspects of the tour together.

Having spent the preceding days learning about LG’s history, exploring its manufacturing facilities and experiencing its smart home technologies, visiting the flagship store offered another opportunity to interact with the brand’s innovations in one space.

One of my favourite experiences there was the Vision Hall.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija)

Stepping into the space felt like stepping into another world. The colours, visuals and immersive displays created such a beautiful cinematic experience. It was almost otherworldly, and I found myself completely immersed in the moment.

Beyond the visual experience, it made me appreciate how far technology has come and the possibilities that innovation continues to create.

It was one of those experiences that was difficult to put into words, so naturally, I had to make a little movie out of it!

PART TWO: EXPLORING KOREA

Beyond the LG tour, one of the things I was most excited about was getting to experience South Korea for myself. Having watched Korean dramas and seen so much of the country’s culture through films and social media, being there in person was a different kind of excitement.

From the streets and shopping districts to the food and everyday lifestyle, there was always something new to discover. And, of course, I came prepared to try the food!

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija)

A Taste of Korea: From Tteokbokki to Bibimbap

One of my favourite parts of exploring Korea was finally getting to try some of the dishes I had only seen in movies and television shows.

First on my list was Tteokbokki, Korea’s popular spicy rice cake dish. Seeing it in Korean dramas had always made me curious, and getting to try it in person was quite an experience.

I also tried Bibimbap, a traditional Korean rice dish served with an assortment of vegetables, toppings and sauce, usually mixed together before eating.

Another highlight was the Korean hot pot rice, which was such a lovely experience. I was particularly excited to try this popular dish and enjoyed getting to share the experience with my audience.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija)

And then there was the banana iced coffee!

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija)

I had heard about Korea’s convenience-store coffee culture, so I had to get myself one. It was one of those little things I was determined to experience as soon as I arrived.

Sometimes, it is the simplest discoveries that become some of your favourite travel memories.

Myeongdong Night Market: Street Food, Shopping and Everything In Between

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija)


If there was one place that gave me a real taste of Seoul’s lively street culture, it was the Myeongdong Night Market.

The atmosphere was everything! From the colourful food stalls and busy walkways to the shops and endless things to explore, it was such an exciting place to spend an evening.

And you certainly cannot visit a Korean night market without trying some street food.

I got to sample Korean rice cakes, cheese hot dogs and octopus fish cakes, among other interesting treats. There was always something new to see, smell or taste, and I loved being able to experience it all.

It was also a lovely opportunity to explore some of the local shops, take in the atmosphere and enjoy the city at night.

After a full day of activities with the LG team, ending the evening in Myeongdong was exactly what I needed.

A Little Korean Shopping Guide

Another experience I enjoyed was exploring Korean malls. If you ever find yourself shopping in South Korea, there are a few things I would recommend adding to your list. First, explore the skincare stores. Korea has a thriving beauty industry, and there are so many interesting products to discover.

Next, find yourself a cute coffee spot. You will find plenty of lovely cafés and interesting coffee options to try. Then, get yourself something fluffy! From furry mini bags to cute accessories, there are so many fun fashion finds to explore.

Don’t forget to pick up a tote bag as well. It’s a practical little souvenir and something you can actually use long after your trip.

And finally, give yourself time to window-shop. Explore the stores, discover new brands, and enjoy the experience without feeling like you have to buy everything.

One more tip: if you’re an eligible foreign visitor, remember to ask about tax refunds on qualifying purchases at participating stores.

A Little Cultural Moment at Gyeongbokgung Palace

No trip to South Korea would feel complete without experiencing a little of its history and traditional culture.

One of the experiences I was particularly looking forward to was visiting Gyeongbokgung Palace, one of Seoul’s most iconic historical landmarks.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija)

And, of course, I couldn’t pass up the opportunity to wear a Hanbok!

The traditional Korean outfit is such a beautiful part of the country’s cultural identity, and getting to dress up and experience the palace in one felt like a lovely way to round off my time in South Korea.

After days of exploring modern technology, futuristic spaces, and innovative experiences, it was wonderful to make room for something that connected me to Korea’s history and heritage.

It was a reminder that there is so much more to a destination than the places we visit. Sometimes, the most memorable experiences come from immersing ourselves in the culture and traditions that make a place unique.

Five Days, So Many Memories

Looking back, my five days in South Korea were everything I hoped they would be and so much more.

From learning about LG’s innovation journey and seeing how AI and robotics are transforming manufacturing, to exploring smart homes, meeting Clyde and experiencing the immersive Vision Hall, the LG tour gave me a much deeper appreciation of the future of technology.

But beyond the learning, there were the people, the conversations, the new connections, the food, the shopping and the beautiful moments of discovering a country I had wanted to visit for so long.

I returned with more than photographs and videos. I left with new perspectives, meaningful connections and a renewed appreciation for how innovation can make a difference in our everyday lives.

South Korea was so good to me, and LG was an incredible host. It was a fulfilling experience, and I genuinely wouldn’t have had it any other way.

Until next time, South Korea. 감사합니다!

For more, visit @bellanaija using the hashtags #BNinSouthKorea and #BNTravels.

item.content:encoded:
Two people engaging with technology in a contemporary hotel lobby work setting.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is changing how people learn, work, communicate and solve problems. In today’s world, if you’re not on board with AI, it could be said you’re being resistant to the fastest-growing technological innovation in the world. From students researching academic subjects to professionals developing business ideas, AI tools have become companions in everyday activities for people. They can help save time, explore new ideas, understand difficult concepts and approach tasks differently.

However, as more people embrace these AI tools, it is important to understand that using AI effectively goes beyond knowing what prompts to enter. It requires knowing when to use it, how to question its responses and, most importantly, when to rely on your own knowledge and judgement.

AI could make us better at what we do, not make us dependent on it.

Here are ways we think you use AI effectively:

Use AI as a Research Assistant

One of the most effective ways to use AI is for research and information gathering. Whether you are writing an article, preparing a presentation or exploring an unfamiliar subject, AI can help you identify relevant topics, explain complex ideas and suggest areas worth investigating.

You can ask it to break down unfamiliar concepts, identify key questions, or suggest research directions. However, do not treat every response as fact. Verify important information using credible sources, published research, books and reliable websites. AI can help you find information, but you are responsible for establishing what is true.

Use AI to Brainstorm and Explore Ideas

Like knowledge gathering, AI can brainstorm ideas with you. Sometimes, the hardest part of starting a project is knowing where to begin. AI can help you overcome this challenge by suggesting ideas, exploring different approaches and presenting perspectives you may not have considered.

For writers, entrepreneurs, researchers and creatives, it can be a useful brainstorming partner. You can share an idea, ask questions about its strengths and weaknesses, and explore ways to develop it. However, brainstorming should not become an excuse to surrender your imagination. Let AI expand your thinking, not replace it.

Use AI to Improve Your Work, Not Replace Your Skills

This is becoming more important.

AI can help you identify grammatical errors, improve sentence construction, organise information, summarise lengthy documents and make your communication clearer. It can reduce the time spent on repetitive tasks and create more room for important responsibilities.

The important thing is that you should remain actively involved. Read what AI produces, question its suggestions and make the final decisions yourself. Your skills improve when you practise them, not when you consistently hand them over to a machine. For students, AI can explain difficult topics and provide feedback on your work.

Protect Your Creativity and Intellectual Independence

It is not advised to outsource your knowledge, original thinking or creativity to AI and then present its output as entirely your own. When students submit assignments generated by AI without engaging in the intellectual effort themselves, they undermine the true purpose of education. When writers publish AI-generated ideas as if they are personal experiences or original thoughts, they misrepresent their contributions to creativity. When professionals rely entirely on AI to perform tasks that they are expected to understand, they compromise the integrity of their work.

There is nothing inherently wrong with seeking assistance. The ethical problem is when assistance becomes substitution, particularly when you claim credit for work, knowledge or experiences that are not yours. Your ideas, experiences, perspective and ability to think independently are valuable. Do not surrender them for convenience.

AI could be considered not the enemy of human intelligence, creativity or productivity. Well, it did not create itself. If used responsibly, it can help learn faster, work smarter, explore opportunities and achieve things that might otherwise take considerably more time.

But the goal should not be to become someone who cannot work without AI. Let AI assist your thinking, not do all your thinking. Let it improve your work, not become the source of all your work. Use it to research and learn. Whatever it is you’re learning – coding, digital marketing, photography, data analysis or another language – you can use AI to structure your learning journey. It can create a beginner-friendly curriculum, recommend practical exercises and assess your progress.

But never allow the convenience of artificial intelligence to make you neglect the value of your own intelligence.

Passport Legacy under the division of the Passport Legacy Group is a leading firm that specializes in global citizenship, residency, international real estate, and corporate solutions like company setup, hosted an intimate cocktail evening featuring Special Guest Thomas Anthony, CEO of IMA Grenada. The event gathered founders, executives, and everyday professionals to explore generational wealth protection, strategic investments, and second citizenship opportunities.


The evening commenced with a welcome address delivered by Weyinmi Oritsejiafor, Managing Director of Passport Legacy Nigeria setting the tone for the night and reaffirming the firm’s commitment to providing tailored advisory services to forward-thinking individuals.


“At Passport Legacy, We are a Swiss owned advisory. We do much more than Passports. We do investment migration and government advisory” Oritsejiafor said, emphasizing that when global mobility is crucial for families and businesses to safeguard their wealth, protect their assets against volatility, and scale internationally, investment migration is a secure foundation for long-term growth.

Oritsejiafor also highlighted that the Passport Legacy Group offers access to international real estate opportunities across key hubs such as Cyprus, Greece, Thailand, Bali, and Dubai. Beyond private advisory, she noted that the firm delivers government advisory services through specialized programs and framework tools, citing their engagement with the government of São Tomé and Príncipe as a key example of this institutional work.


The centerpiece of the evening was a keynote presentation by Special Guest Thomas Anthony, CEO of the Investment Migration Agency Grenada (IMA Grenada). Anthony shared key insights into Grenada’s premier Citizenship by Investment (CBI) framework, detailing its unique economic advantages, tax efficiencies, and strategic global access for business owners and proactive individuals.

Anthony highlighted that Grenada’s Investment Migration framework delivers a transparent gateway for global flexibility and security. The road to the 75th Miss Universe crown is officially underway, and Nigeria’s representative, Dr Danielle Adewusi, has touched down in San Juan, Puerto Rico, to begin pre-pageant activities.

Before taking the national crown, she placed in the Top 5 at Miss Universe Great Britain in 2023 and completed international runway coaching in Thailand. With recent updates by the Miss Universe Organisation removing maximum age limits, 29-year-old Danielle is also among the delegates competing under the expanded eligibility rules.

Arriving in San Juan on Monday, 9 November, Danielle joins nearly 120 delegates from across the globe for preliminary rounds, national costume presentations, and rehearsals.

item.content:encoded:
In a city where creativity is a culture and every corner has a story to tell, Heineken brought another expression of Lagos to life at Lagos Fashion Week 2026. Through its City of Cities: Where Taste Rules experience, the brand transformed its eleven-year partnership with the fashion showcase into a celebration of the people, ideas, and experiences shaping the city’s creative identity, bringing fashion, music, innovation, and social connections together across the week.

From runway presentations to the Heineken Lounge, the debut of Heineken Studio, and an energetic after-party, the brand created experiences that went beyond the collections on display, inviting guests to explore new expressions of taste, discover creative possibilities, and connect over shared interests.

At the heart of the experience was City of Cities: Where Taste Rules, an experience inspired by the many influences that make Lagos what it is. First introduced in 2025, the concept recognises that Lagos is more than one city; it is a melting pot of different cultures, communities, sounds, and styles. At Lagos Fashion Week 2026, Heineken brought this idea into focus, celebrating the diversity of expression that makes the city’s creative scene distinct.

The experience also marked another chapter in Heineken’s eleven-year journey with Lagos Fashion Week. Over the years, the partnership has explored the intersection of fashion, craftsmanship, and taste through initiatives such as Woven Threads in 2022, the Dyelab collaboration in 2023, and the H45 Collection in 2024, before introducing City of Cities: Where Taste Rules in 2025. Each edition has created a new way to engage with fashion and culture, with this year’s experience building on that foundation through fresh expressions of creativity and innovation.

Aligned with the 2026 theme, CRAFTED: Heritage. Innovation. Circular Futures, Heineken’s presence celebrated the artistry, intentionality, and evolving perspectives shaping contemporary fashion. Across the venue, guests arrived in style, adding their own interpretations of fashion and self-expression to the atmosphere. The Heineken Lounge provided a space to unwind, exchange ideas, and connect as guests enjoyed chilled Heineken, refreshments, and the runway presentations. The experience also offered a taste of something different, with guests exploring Foam Infusions in exciting variations, including espresso and blood orange.

A major highlight was the Nigerian debut of Heineken Studio, the brand’s Playground of Innovation, which brought together taste, creativity, and personal expression in an interactive space. Beyond discovering new ways to experience lager through Foam Infusions, guests could step into the painting studio to create personalised designs on their own Heineken cans. The photo area and Heineken-branded backdrops also became popular spots for guests to capture their moments, express their individual styles, and share their experiences. Through these interactive touchpoints, Heineken Studio gave attendees more than something to discover; it gave them something to create and make their own.

The ‘City of Cities’ runway experience brought another dimension to the week’s celebration of craftsmanship and creative heritage. Opening with This Is Us, a poetry presentation by Anjola Adebayo exploring the history and processes behind indigenous textile making, the Heineken runway showcase placed cultural storytelling at the heart of fashion. The presentation included a heartwarming musical performance, setting the tone as models took to the runway to showcase the collections. It was a compelling expression of the relationship between heritage, artistry, and contemporary design, reflecting the spirit of this year’s CRAFTED theme.

As the runway moments gave way to the night’s rhythm, Heineken extended the celebration with the Heineken Studio after-party. The energy was building from the entrance, with DJ sets and Hypeman Best getting the crowd moving alongside dancers. Glowsticks, vibrant lighting, and an enthusiastic audience added to the atmosphere, turning the space into a lively celebration of music and self-expression. The entertainment lineup kept the momentum going, with Hypeman Best setting things in motion, LOUD Urban Choir bringing their musical magic, and DJ Spinall, DJ Consequence, Shody the Turn Up King, DJ Stormy, and DJ Brightstar taking the energy to another level. From the performances to the dancefloor moments, the after-party brought guests together for an energetic close to the fashion week experience.

Speaking on the experience, Sandra Amachree, Head of Marketing Communications at Nigerian Breweries Plc, said:

“For over a decade, our partnership with Heineken Lagos Fashion Week has grown alongside the creative community, creating opportunities to celebrate fashion, culture, and the people driving both forward. This year, through City of Cities: Where Taste Rules, we set out to create an experience that captured the spirit of Lagos and its diverse expressions of creativity. The Nigerian debut of Heineken Studio gave us an exciting opportunity to bring this vision to life in a more immersive way, allowing guests to explore their creativity, discover new expressions of taste, and connect with one another. Seeing people engage with these experiences and make them their own was particularly rewarding. It speaks to what we continue to champion: creating meaningful spaces where culture, creativity, and connection come together to inspire memorable experiences.”

As the curtain comes down on Heineken Lagos Fashion Week 2026, Heineken’s City of Cities: Where Taste Rules leaves behind a celebration of what happens when different worlds meet. From personalised creative experiences and indigenous fashion heritage to experimental taste, music, and unforgettable social moments, the experience reinforced a simple idea: in a city as dynamic as Lagos, there is always another expression to discover and another reason to come together.

item.title: 5 New Albums to Listen to This Week: Skepta, Phyno, Ty Bello & More
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.description:
New album releases from Skepta (The Fork & Knife), Phyno (Let That Sink In), Ty Bello (I Speak Lion / I Speak Lamb), Anendlessocean (Freedom), and Tobe Nwigwe (The Bridge) span Afrobeats, UK rap, indigenous hip-hop, and alternative gospel.

The post 5 New Albums to Listen to This Week: Skepta, Phyno, Ty Bello & More appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
Skepta holding the official clear vinyl edition of his sixth studio album, The Fork and Knife. Photo Credit: Skepta/Instagram 

Your playlist could do with a little shake-up, and these five albums might be exactly what it needs. Skepta is reconnecting with his roots, Phyno is giving us more of the indigenous rap we love, Ty Bello has two albums exploring different expressions of worship, and Anendlessocean and Tobe Nwigwe are taking their sounds in interesting directions. From UK grime and Nigerian hip-hop to alternative gospel and soul, there’s a lot to discover across these new releases.

Whether you’re in the mood for bars, worship, thoughtful songwriting or music that brings different cultures together, this week’s selection has something worth hearing.

Skepta: The Fork & Knife

Back in 2012, Skepta found himself at odds with a corporatised grime scene, sparking a pivotal career reckoning that eventually led to his landmark 2016 album Konnichiwa. On his long-awaited 15-track sixth album, The Fork & Knife, the 44-year-old MC reflects on his journey as grime’s most influential elder statesman and the son of Nigerian immigrants.

Named after his mother’s favourite proverb, the record is a deep exploration of identity and perseverance. Musically, Skepta bridges continents by blending global diasporic sounds. He teams up with Aya Nakamura on the zouk-infused “Chippie”, taps Asake for the Afrobeats crossover “Aloe Vera”, and recruits Chase & Status alongside Suggs for the sharp single “Innocent Smile”. The project closes with “Belly”, an eight-minute masterclass featuring Boy Better Know members Jme and Frisco.

Phyno: Let That Sink In

Arriving nearly 10 years after his groundbreaking sophomore record The Playmaker, Phyno’s 15-track sixth solo album, Let That Sink In (LTSI), showcases his timeless command of indigenous rap. Across the record,the Enugu-born star blends soul, R&B, and traditional Nigerian sounds to explore faith, resilience, and personal evolution.

The album features powerhouse collaborations, including Seyi Vibez on the opener “Ndu Ka Aku”, Fireboy DML on “I Believe”, and Jeriq on “Ije Enu”. Whether taking the government to task on “20 Years to Come” or offering uplifting anthems like “Chukwu Okike”, Phyno proves why he remains a definitive voice in African hip-hop.

Ty Bello: I Speak Lion and I Speak Lamb

Creative powerhouse Ty Bello delivers a massive double-album listening experience with I Speak Lion and I Speak Lamb. Split into two distinct spiritual volumes, the expansive project captures both the bold, triumphant authority of worship and its quiet, intimate moments.

I Speak Lion leans into explosive, high-energy sounds designed to spark courage, featuring powerful pairings with Sunmisola Agbebi, Greatman Takit, and Limoblaze. In contrast, I Speak Lamb steps into soaking acoustic textures and tender devotional spaces, offering a complete, multi-layered sanctuary for listeners.

Anendlessocean: Freedom

Alternative Afro-Gospel innovator Anendlessocean expands his personal sonic universe on his full-length studio album, Freedom. Building on the strong momentum of fan-favourite singles like “Promises”, the 14-track project weaves contemporary R&B grooves with uncompromised spiritual messaging.

Highlighted by lush vocal harmonies and atmospheric production on tracks like “Speak On It” with Ryan Ofei and “Let the Church Say” with Wale Adenuga, the album solidifies his unique lane. It stands as a defining milestone for listeners seeking modern alternative soul paired with deep introspection.

Tobe Nwigwe & Fat Nwigwe: The Bridge

Houston-born artist Tobe Nwigwe embraces every corner of his heritage on his 12-track collaborative album with his wife, Fat Nwigwe, titled The Bridge. Raised in Alief by Igbo parents from southeastern Nigeria, Tobe seamlessly fuses heavy Texas trap basslines with traditional Nigerian percussion and vocal samples across the project.

The record boasts an impressive lineup, featuring Houston legend Paul Wall, international heavyweights Labrinth and Sia, and hip-hop icons Busta Rhymes and Malice alongside Nigerian acts like Flavour, ODUMODUBLVCK, and The Cavemen. Anchored by Fat Nwigwe’s commanding vocals, the album is a triumphant celebration of holding two cultural truths in one body.

item.content:encoded:
During Lagos Fashion Week, The Ladymaker’s Founder and Creative Director, Ifeyinwa Azubike, introduced Stand On Ceremony, a collection that considers the relationship between personal expression and the expectations attached to an occasion.

Presented on 27 October 2026 at The Sphere, Lagos, the collection draws from the familiar expression to stand on ceremony: to insist on the observance of formalities. For Ifeyinwa Azubike, the idea presents an opportunity to examine the traditions women inherit, the rituals they observe and the choices they make when dressing for themselves.

The collection is built around two identities: The Devotee and The Rebel. They are not opposing personalities so much as two ways of relating to ceremony.

The Devotee embraces its rituals. She understands the language of formal dressing and participates in it with intention. For her, dressing fully is an expression of desire and personal conviction. The Rebel is equally familiar with the rules, but she is selective about the ones she follows. Her approach to dressing allows for disruption, though never simply for the sake of attention.

Through these characters, Azubike considers a familiar experience for women: the pull between what an occasion expects and what an individual wants to express. Every woman who has dressed for an occasion has encountered this tension in some form, whether in choosing to honour a tradition or finding room to express herself within it.

The garments give form to this conversation. The Cloister Dress is paired with the Banner Dress, while the Manor Jumpsuit is placed alongside the Assembly Set. Other looks, including the Herald Dress, Emissary Set, Procession Dress and Sovereign Set, extend the collection’s exploration of the two identities.

Material choices move between crimson jacquard, rose jacquard, ice jacquard, denim Akwete, wine Adire, midnight sequins and beaded velvet. The collection draws on fabrics and textures that allow ceremony to be interpreted through different moods, silhouettes and degrees of formality.

Stand On Ceremony was presented during Lagos Fashion Week through an intimate fashion presentation, followed by a soirée where guests could experience the garments more closely.

The evening was held in partnership with MAC Cosmetics, which provided beauty; Moët & Chandon, the champagne partner; Jacque Scents, which created the fragrance experience; and The Nail Boutique, responsible for nail artistry.

For Ifeyinwa Azubike, the question the collection leaves with its audience is a personal one: are you a Rebel or a Devotee?

The Ladymaker Brand Profile

Founded in 2015 by Ifeyinwa Azubike, The Ladymaker is a Lagos-based womenswear brand that brings together African heritage, classical elegance and contemporary design. Established by Azubike following a career in commercial law, the brand was born from a desire to create timeless clothing rooted in craftsmanship, fit and enduring style rather than fleeting trends.

At the heart of The Ladymaker is a belief that heritage is a living source of inspiration. The brand draws from centuries-old African textile traditions, artisanal techniques and cultural references, reinterpreting them through refined silhouettes designed for the modern woman. Rather than treating craft as decoration, The Ladymaker integrates it into the construction of each garment, creating pieces that balance tradition with contemporary dressing.

Every design is meticulously handmade in Lagos by a team of pan-African artisans, reflecting the brand’s commitment to craftsmanship, quality and thoughtful production. Techniques such as handwoven aso oke, shibori-inspired textiles, jacquard weaving and artisanal finishing regularly appear throughout its collections, demonstrating a considered approach to both material and form.

The Ladymaker has become recognised for dressing women through life’s meaningful moments, offering wardrobes that move effortlessly across work, celebrations, travel, weddings and special occasions. Its collections are defined by elegant tailoring, architectural silhouettes and versatile pieces that remain relevant well beyond a single season.

item.content:encoded:
Africa’s tech icon and Chairman of Zinox Group, Leo Stan Ekeh, has told an international gathering of women leaders that his decision to build a technology company in Africa, at a time when the sector was virtually non-existent on the continent, amounted to what he described as “corporate suicide”.

Speaking on the theme “Losing the Fear”, at The International Women Leadership Conference (TIWLC) in Dubai, organised by the Ibukun Awosika Leadership Foundation, Ekeh, who was a keynote speaker on the final day of this year’s conference, addressed over 600 women industry leaders from different countries across the globe. He said he returned from his studies abroad to a Nigeria where his peers were filing into banking, oil and gas, and where technology was largely seen as a foreign game.

Ekeh, who studied Economics in India, said he was discouraged from pursuing a postgraduate degree in Computer Science in Europe because of the prevailing perception then that Africa might have little need for computers over the next 35 years, potentially leaving him frustrated. He subsequently opted for a postgraduate degree in Risk Management before pursuing a Master’s degree in Business Law (LLM) at London Guildhall University. He recalled that he could not sit his final law examinations because he had diverted his tuition fees into his passion for technology entrepreneurship. He also disclosed that he had fended off recruitment attempts by international technology companies that had sought to hire him before his return to Africa.

“I chose the road not taken,” he told the conference. “It was corporate suicide in the eyes of my parents and many others. I lost the fear because I believed technology was the master key that would unlock possibilities for Nigeria and Africa.”

He said the journey came with considerable hardship, including living on one meal a day for over three years and sleeping in a very small room in his office.

According to him, his vision was to create a Nigerian and, by extension, an African IT identity. Recalling the launch of his first company, Task Systems Ltd, over 35 years ago, the company that pioneered desktop publishing and computer graphics in Nigeria.
At the launch, held at the Sheraton Hotel, Ikeja, Ekeh recalled addressing an overcrowded hall filled with industry leaders, some of whom were seeing computers for the first time. He told them: “No country can claim to be independent without technology independence.”

He said the Nigerian media embraced the vision, describing him as a “miracle child” and supporting the company’s roadmap. This, he noted, contributed to the computerisation of over 97 per cent of media and multimedia houses in Nigeria, as well as in other African countries.

He further explained that the decision to establish Zinox Technologies, which became one of Africa’s first Microsoft WHQL- and Intel-certified computer manufacturers, was driven by the need to give Nigeria and Africa a global technology identity.

“We were not just building computers,” he said. “We were building a statement that Africa could manufacture to global standards because we had the passion, experience and capacity, and believed the risk was worth taking. The government and people of Nigeria celebrated us. With Zinox, we demystified and domesticated technology and were able to handle critical projects in Nigeria and some African countries. This is what innovation is all about.”

Ekeh, however, did not present the journey as a smooth one. He told the women that Nigeria had both “blessed and bruised” him, and spoke about what he described as controversial patronage, corporate blackmail and the battles that come with building a visible business in a challenging environment. He said these experiences explain why many billionaires in Africa may be unwilling to endure the difficulties associated with building businesses and may struggle to defend their wealth.

“Fear will always have a voice,” he said. “But it must not have a vote. The road less travelled is less travelled for a reason. It is harder. It is lonelier. But it is worth it.”
He assured the women that he would tell the full story in his forthcoming book before the end of 2027.

Ekeh, who reminded the women that they hold the comprehensive keys to national prosperity in this second quarter of the 21st century, also highlighted his group’s investment in women in technology.

According to him, TD Africa Distributions Ltd, one of Africa’s biggest technology distribution companies, has, through its TecHerdemy initiative, trained over 1,000 women in cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, software development, data science and professional etiquette. Many of the graduates now occupy leadership roles across the technology ecosystem.

He added that women also occupy strategic positions within the Zinox Group, including several female chief executives leading business units.

Addressing the women at the conference, Ekeh encouraged them to recognise their capacity to shape industries, create opportunities and influence the future. His message resonated with the wider conversation around women’s leadership, economic participation and the need for greater representation in sectors traditionally dominated by men.

He underscored the importance of courage, competence and determination, particularly for women seeking to break barriers in business and technology. He also stressed that leadership goes beyond personal achievement; it involves creating pathways through which others can advance.

The conference, convened by the Ibukun Awosika Leadership Foundation, brought together women founders, executives and first-time managing directors from across Africa and beyond.

item.content:encoded:
Midea is introducing the Space Master Refrigerator to Nigerian consumers, placing practical food storage at the centre of its “More Room for Nigeria” campaign. The introduction speaks to a familiar household situation: a major grocery shop, a weekend of hosting or a family celebration can quickly turn refrigerator space into a daily planning challenge.

Space Master is presented with a simple proposition: “Same Size. More Space. More Capacity.” Its approach to storage design gives households more usable interior space for the food, drinks and everyday essentials they need to keep at home.

For households planning meals ahead, the practical question is not only what to buy, but where everything will go. Fresh produce, bottled drinks, ingredients for family meals and food prepared for guests all compete for space. Space Master’s bigger-capacity proposition gives consumers more room to accommodate larger grocery shops, everyday essentials and food for family occasions, helping households prepare more comfortably for both daily routines and celebrations.

“More Room for Nigeria” connects that functional product story to everyday Nigerian life. From stocking up for a busy working week to preparing for a family gathering, the campaign shows why usable storage matters at moments when households need flexibility. Its companion message, “Every Celebration Needs More Room,”

gives the product a role in the preparations for the occasion — before guests arrive, meals are served and memories are made.

The campaign also places product discovery at the heart of the consumer experience. Through planned retail demonstrations, shoppers will be invited to open the Space Master, explore its interior layout and see examples of how groceries and meal-preparation items can be arranged. The “Grocery Fit Challenge” and household grocery scenarios are designed to make the storage proposition tangible, while store representatives can answer model-specific questions and explain the purchase process.

Secrets have a way of coming out, family ties can get complicated, and love doesn’t always go according to plan. These are just some of the stories unfolding in this week’s Nollywood releases on YouTube. From psychological drama and riverine mysteries to corporate battles and family betrayals, here are five films bringing different stories to the screen.

7 Years Silence (Bolaji Ogunmola TV)

What happens when a web of long-kept secrets finally unravels after nearly a decade? 7 Years Silence follows a devoted wife who, after seven years of marriage and a painful struggle to conceive, discovers her seemingly perfect husband has been living a complete double life. As hidden motives and suppressed truths explode into the open, every character is forced to face the shattering fallout of a marriage built on an illusion.

This gripping emotional thriller features standout performances by BamBam (Bamike Olawunmi–Adenibuyan), Deyemi Okanlawon, and Teniola Aladese.

The River Remembers (Omoni Oboli TV)

Love and dark ancestral secrets collide in this haunting riverine drama. Newly engaged Morayo and Akindele travel to his hometown to celebrate their future, but beside a forbidden river, Morayo’s recurring nightmares begin to unearth a devastating truth. As painful revelations draw an unyielding line between their families, the couple is forced to choose between their dream together or losing each other to a past they never chose.

Produced by Nollywood powerhouse Omoni Oboli, the movie stars Taye Arimoro, Teniola Aladese, Kunle Omisore, Najite Dede, Olami Samuel, Bridget John, Oyetola Elemosho, Tolu Otebiyi, Paul Word, Taiwo Familoni.

Caught in the Cycle (Biodun Stephen TV)

Tackling heavy themes of trauma, broken trust, and survival, Caught in the Cycle delivers an intense psychological ride. The narrative centers on a gifted teenage girl whose life takes a terrifying turn after she is taken in by a wealthy couple promising her a brighter future. Instead of sanctuary, she finds herself trapped in a living nightmare of abuse, manipulation, and betrayal—ultimately leading to a shocking crime that forces her to fight with everything she has for her freedom and the truth.

Directed by Olubunmi Akingbola and produced by Biodun Stephen, the film relies on raw, high-stakes performances from an impressive cast starring Stan Nze, Angel Unigwe, and Leolidas Ewane.

User Friendly (RuthKadiri247)

High-stakes corporate greed meets unexpected romance in User Friendly. Following her father’s death, billionaire heiress Tenny (Ruth Kadiri) struggles to take charge of his business empire as alcohol abuse and poor choices make her a prime target for manipulative relatives. To protect her, her grandmother hires Morris (Maurice Sam), a firm bodyguard tasked with shielding her from family sabotage. As Morris helps her navigate the corporate snakes, their professional bond evolves into a deep romance that reshapes her future.

Helmed by Ruth Kadiri, the film stars Ruth Kadiri and Maurice Sam, alongside Fessa Okafor, Betty Ndidiamaka Okafor Ajoku, and Anthony Woode.

Beyond Blood (Uche Montana TV)

Closing out this week’s recommendations is Beyond Blood, a story that proves the people we trust the most can often become the source of our deepest pain. Driven by bitter betrayals, hidden motives, and a desperate craving for vengeance, the film examines how far someone will push past boundaries to make things right when blood ties turn toxic. It is a high-drama narrative packed with explosive family conflicts, emotional struggles, and unexpected twists.

Directed by Ben Cassie, the project relies on intense onscreen chemistry between Uche Montana and Nollywood veteran Emeka Ike alongside a dynamic supporting cast.

item.title: Nkanyeziyethu Malunga: The Zimbabwean Designer Preserving African Heritage Through Fashion
item.dc:creator: Bird
item.description:
Sebele feels that this work has applications beyond fashion, such as cultural tourism, research, and creative enterprise. Its significance stems from making indigenous knowledge visible, as well as demonstrating how it may be used to inform future research and commercial activities.

The post Nkanyeziyethu Malunga: The Zimbabwean Designer Preserving African Heritage Through Fashion appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
At her workshop in Bulawayo, Zimbabwe, Nkanyeziyethu Malunga crafted colour into fabric, using plants, tree bark and other natural materials gathered from the environment. Choosing a colour or designing a pattern is only one of the processes. Each material carries details on how it was gathered, prepared, and transformed, which Malunga is incorporating into contemporary fashion.

“My dyes are mainly extracted from plants such as mnyii and hibiscus. Although I also use many other plants, including tubers, that have properties suitable for dye extraction. I love hibiscus not only for its petals, which produce beautiful dyes, but also for its tea.”

The 37-year-old designer is challenging conventional notions about what defines a fashion collection and where creative knowledge originates. Through her clothing business, GANU, she transforms indigenous materials and skills into clothes and accessories, demonstrating how knowledge passed down through generations can inform modern design, provide opportunities for rural women, and conserve cultural practices.

Her method is based on teachings learned from her late maternal grandmother, Ngatsha Nkatha, who resided in Tsholotsho, a rural district in Zimbabwe. During the school vacations, Malunga and her siblings traveled from Bulawayo to visit grandma, witnessing as she turned sisal, sedge, and reeds into winnowing baskets.

“When I was a child, I often visited my grandmother in the village with my siblings. She was very dexterous with her fingers, and that passion eventually became mutual.”

Malunga started experimenting with fashion in her teens before launching Ganu in 2013. The name is derived from iganu, the Ndebele term for marula fruit, and represents her connection to local resources and African identity. Her creations blend basketry, crocheting, batik, and beadwork with natural dyes, leather, and other locally produced materials.

For Malunga, the importance of these materials goes beyond their appearance. Bamboo, sisal, reeds, and sedge are used in basketry, and she breeds Angora goats for their fur, which she straightens and dyes to make garments. Cowhide obtained from local abattoirs is softened in a tannery before being mixed into leather designs.

“I keep Angora goats for the fur needed in garment production. However, for raw materials such as cowhide, I usually source these from local abattoirs while sisal and tree barks are either harvested by me or sometimes extracted by colleagues I work with, who are based in the rural areas.”

Desmond Ntini, a cultural entrepreneur based in Bulawayo, sees Malunga’s work as part of a broader shift in how African history is perceived and used.

” Malunga is redefining the fashion industry by blending traditional African influences with contemporary creativity. Her work explains how our cultural identity can inspire modern designs while opening doors for sustainable fashion, business opportunities, and the celebration of African heritage.” Ntini said.

Her ventures also go beyond her own label. In 2024, she founded Matobo Goes Fashion And Beyond, working with Matobo women in partnership with Ekhaya-gaia, my beautiful home in Zimbabwe, and the Amagugu International Heritage Centre. The concept transforms traditional hut paintings into contemporary clothes.

The project addresses the issue of cultural preservation. Rain can remove paintings from traditional dwellings, putting communities at risk of losing patterns that are not often documented. Reproducing these designs on fabric provides another way to record and disseminate them, as well as introduce the patterns to audiences outside of the communities where they originated.

The initiative also provides opportunities for women to share their knowledge and engage in the interpretation of their cultural legacy. Rather than interpreting traditional decoration as something that solely belongs in rural dwellings, the concept incorporates it into a new context while maintaining its connection to the communities that created it.

This approach opens up the possibility of adding value to Zimbabwe’s resources and abilities rather than regarding them as apart from the official fashion sector.

Zimbabwe’s cultural and creative industries contributed an estimated US$2.7 billion to the country’s economy in 2024, equivalent to 5.92% of gross domestic product, according to a study whose findings were reported in June 2026. The sector accounted for an estimated 22,223 jobs.

Dr. Florence Sebele, a senior lecturer and acting chair of the Department of Art, Design, and Technology Education at the National University of Science and Technology in Bulawayo, studies indigenous knowledge in textile technology. She sees Malunga’s method as an opportunity to challenge assumptions about African creativity.

“By taking indigenous knowledge that has long been undervalued and transforming it into modern fashion, Malunga speaks to our identity, culture and heritage as Zimbabweans and also as Africans. Her work is a powerful reminder that we have so much to take pride in, while for the wider world, it challenges the dominant narrative of what fashion is and where innovation comes from, showing that authentic, rooted African knowledge has global relevance.”

That dilemma is especially important in an industry where African cultural references can be seen on international runways yet the expertise and people that support them receive little recognition. Malunga’s work begins with techniques and materials rooted in local culture and then adapts them for modern applications.

Sebele feels that this work has applications beyond fashion, such as cultural tourism, research, and creative enterprise. Its significance stems from making indigenous knowledge visible, as well as demonstrating how it may be used to inform future research and commercial activities.

Malunga’s grandmother died before she could pass on everything she knew, leaving Malunga to seek out other custodians of traditional skills.

“My grandmother’s death came early, before I could master everything on the use of indigenous knowledge in creating contemporary fashion. As a result, I have also learned to tap into the wisdom of various elderly women that I have come across since embarking on this journey.”

Her creations have been showcased on platforms beyond Zimbabwe, including the Durban Fashion Fair in South Africa in 2016. She was nominated for Outstanding Fashion Designer at the 2018 Bulawayo Arts Awards and has worked with markets in Ghana, Europe, and the United States. She displayed under the ZimTrade pavilion at the Zimbabwe International Trade Fair in April of this year, and the organisation’s SheExports initiative has helped her explore international markets.

However, the greater relevance of Malunga’s work rests in what occurs before a garment reaches a buyer. Plant dyes, basketry skills, traditional paintings, and rural women’s expertise all contribute to a creative process that bridges generations and creates new avenues for cultural expression.

“…we learn everyday, we learn as we go, and we learn from everyone,”Malunga reflected.

Malunga’s challenge is to ensuring that this expertise is retained, that the communities that contribute to it are acknowledged, and that the opportunities it offers extend beyond the runway.

item.title: History in Morocco! How Nigeria’s Flamingos Won the World Cup
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.category: FIFA U17 Womens World Cup Morocco 2026
item.description:
Nigeria’s Flamingos won the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup in Morocco, defeating Japan 2–1 in the final to become the first African nation to lift a FIFA women's trophy.

The post History in Morocco! How Nigeria’s Flamingos Won the World Cup appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
The Flamingos celebrate on stage with green and white confetti as they lift the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup trophy.

History was made in Rabat as the Flamingos of Nigeria conquered global football at the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup. Under head coach Akeem Busari, the team executed an extraordinary seven-match campaign at the finals, overcoming an early setback to claim six consecutive victories and become the first African nation to lift any FIFA women’s international trophy.

Midfielder Oluebube Umejiaku earned individual recognition by winning the FIFA Golden Ball as the Player of the Tournament alongside Player of the Match honors in the final. The squad also displayed exceptional attacking breadth, scoring goals through eight different players across seven matches at the finals while registering over 100 goal attempts.

Oluebube Umejiaku poses with the FIFA Golden Ball and Player of the Match awards following Nigeria’s World Cup triumph.

Here is the match-by-match breakdown of how Nigeria navigated the African qualifiers, powered through the World Cup group stage, defeated multi-time global champions in the knockouts, and clinched the ultimate trophy in Morocco.

Nigeria’s Flamingos celebrate becoming the first African nation to win the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup after defeating Japan 2-1 in Rabat.

Phase 1: The African Qualifying Journey

Nigeria entered the African U-17 World Cup qualifying campaign in the second round, establishing dominance in home-and-away aggregate ties across West Africa. The Flamingos opened their qualification run with an emphatic 5–0 away victory in Guinea, led by team captain Harmony Chidi’s first-half hat-trick alongside goals from Oluwakemi Adegbuyi and Mary Dunstan. They followed up with a 7–0 victory in the home leg in Ogun State to complete a 12–0 aggregate shutout.

The Flamingos celebrate on the pitch following their matchday four fixture at the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup.

In the final qualifying round, Nigeria established a three-goal lead in Monrovia by defeating Liberia 4–1, thanks to a brace from Harmony Chidi and goals from Shakirat Moshood and Peace Effiong. Chidi then sealed a 2–0 second-leg win back home to finish the qualifiers with 12 goals and secure Nigeria’s ticket to Morocco.

Phase 2: Group B at the World Cup (Morocco)

Placed in Group B alongside Poland, Puerto Rico, and defending world champions DPR Korea, Nigeria had to battle through one of the tournament’s most competitive pools. The campaign started with a tight 2–1 loss to Poland in Rabat, putting pressure on the team to perform in their remaining fixtures. The Flamingos bounced back immediately with a 2–0 shutout victory over Puerto Rico to claim their first three points.

Nigeria’s Flamingos celebrate their historic 3-1 Group B victory over defending champions DPR Korea in Morocco.

In their final group match, Nigeria produced one of the tournament’s biggest tactical upsets by defeating two-time defending champions DPR Korea 3–1. Goals from Oluwakemi Adegbuyi, Oluebube Umejiaku, and Kanyinsola Yusuf snapped DPR Korea’s long unbeaten regulation-time streak at the U-17 World Cup and sent Nigeria through to the knockouts at the top of Group B on head-to-head tiebreakers.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino presents the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup trophy to Nigeria captain Harmony Chidi alongside CAF President Patrice Motsepe.

Phase 3: The Knockout Stages

Nigeria entered the expanded 16-team knockout rounds, defeating top-tier opponents from CONCACAF, CONMEBOL, and AFC. In the Round of 16, Nigeria put together a strong performance against Mexico, winning 2–1 through goals from Oluebube Umejiaku and Mary Dunstan. The quarter-final against Venezuela proved to be a tense affair, remaining scoreless until the 89th minute when Oluebube Umejiaku won a late penalty.

Nigeria captain Harmony Chidi in action during the Round of 16 as the Flamingos secured a 2-1 victory over Mexico in Morocco

Substitute defender Azeezat Oduntan converted from the spot to send Nigeria to the semi-finals. Facing South American champions Brazil in Rabat, Nigeria broke through in the 56th minute with a strike from Queen Joseph before forward Awawu Bashiru scored twice in the 71st and 80th minutes to lock in a 3–1 win and book Nigeria’s place in the final.

The Final: Nigeria 2–1 Japan

Played at the Mohammed VI Football Complex in Rabat, Morocco, Nigeria claimed the World Cup title with a 2–1 victory over Japan. Awawu Bashiru opened the scoring in the 39th minute with a long-range shot.

Two minutes after half-time, tournament MVP Oluebube Umejiaku doubled the advantage. Japan pulled a goal back through Fuki Ito in the 80th minute, but Nigeria defended their lead through stoppage time to secure the World Cup trophy.

Nigeria’s Flamingos celebrate becoming the first African nation to win the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup after defeating Japan 2-1 in Rabat.

The Flamingos react after earning a spot in the quarter-finals of the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup.

Nigeria’s Flamingos celebrate on the field following their quarter-final win over Venezuela.

As Africa accelerates its digital transformation journey, the conversation is no longer simply about adopting new technologies, it is now about ensuring they are deployed responsibly, governed effectively, and trusted by the people they serve. 

It is against this backdrop that the Eko Innovation Centre, in collaboration with the Lagos State Ministry of Innovation, Science & Technology, announces the 8th edition of the Art of Technology Lagos (AOT Lagos 8.0), scheduled to hold on Thursday, 3 December 2026, at the Landmark Event Centre, Victoria Island, Lagos. 

Now in its eighth year, AOT Lagos has welcomed over 125,000 participants, hosted 340 speakers, delivered 262 keynote sessions, and generated more than 15 million engagements across 145 countries. More importantly, AOT Lagos has evolved beyond a conference into a platform for collaboration and policy development, contributing to landmark initiatives including the Lagos

Innovation Master Plan, Startup Lagos, the Talent Acceleration Masterplan, the Lagos Digital Service Portal, and the Lagos Digital Service Portal 2.0 (Chatbot Inclusive). 

This year’s theme, “Beyond Smart Cities: Tech Adoption × Ethics × Governance,” reflects one of the defining conversations of our time. As artificial intelligence, digital public infrastructure, connected services, and data-driven technologies continue to transform economies and societies, governments and businesses must ensure innovation is underpinned by transparency, accountability, inclusion, and public trust. 

Bringing these critical conversations to the forefront, AOT Lagos 8.0 will feature a distinguished line-up of technology leaders, policymakers, entrepreneurs, and global industry experts, including Dr. Bosun Tijani, the Honourable Minister of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy, Sade Dada, Head of Public Policy, Anglophone West Africa at Meta, Engr. Abisoye Coker-Odusote, Director-General and Chief Executive Officer of the National Identity Management Commission (NIMC), the Honourable Commissioner, Ministry of Innovation, Science and Technology, Lagos State Olatubosun Alake and more. Their participation will bring diverse perspectives to the conference’s central conversations around responsible AI adoption, digital governance, smart infrastructure, the future of work, digital inclusion, and sustainable innovation.

Speaking on this year’s edition, Victor Afolabi, Founder of Eko Innovation Centre, said:

“Technology is changing faster than ever before, but sustainable progress depends on more than innovation alone. It requires responsible adoption, effective governance, and meaningful collaboration across the public and private sectors. AOT Lagos 8.0 provides a platform for the conversations, partnerships, and ideas that will help shape Africa’s digital future.”

This year’s conference will feature executive keynotes, policy dialogues, ministerial roundtables, technology exhibitions, startup showcases, investment engagements, and strategic conversations across eight thematic tracks covering:

  • AI, Ethics & Governance
  • Smart Infrastructure & Urban Innovation
  • Fintech, Regulation & Digital Economy
  • Future of Work & Talent Transformation
  • Digital Identity, Data & Cybersecurity
  • ClimateTech & Sustainable Cities
  • Civic Technology & Digital Inclusion
  • Startup Innovation & Investment

The conference will also host the 5th AOT Ecosystem Awards, recognising outstanding startups, ecosystem builders, policymakers, and organisations driving innovation and digital transformation across Nigeria and the African continent.

Building on seven successful editions, AOT Lagos 8.0 aims to strengthen public-private collaboration, inspire innovative solutions, encourage investment, and generate policy recommendations that support responsible technology adoption and sustainable digital transformation across Africa. 

To learn more or register to attend, visit www.aotlagos.com.

item.content:encoded:
In 2021, I graduated from the University of Ibadan with a degree in Mathematics. I thought my life would be about numbers on a whiteboard. I did not know it would become about numbers in people’s bank accounts, and the fears, hopes and contradictions that sit behind them.

By mid-2023, I had taken a job selling real estate. I started at the very bottom, as a sales development representative: the person who makes the first call, sends the message and follows up when nobody replies. Today, I manage a sales team. Somewhere between then and now, I stopped seeing real estate as a business of land and buildings. I started seeing it as a mirror. Put a property in front of a Nigerian, and you will learn, very quickly, how they think about money.

Here is some of what that mirror has shown me:

A prospect once told me, with complete confidence, “I have my money ready for the land.” We fixed an inspection. We walked the site together under the afternoon sun, red earth on our shoes. Then, standing on the plot, the prospect asked if they could pay next year. I was not angry. I understood. Saying “I am ready” feels good. Being ready is different. It means you have decided what the money is for, and you are willing to let it go.

I have seen versions of that moment many times. The client who books an inspection for 2 pm and is still not there at 4 pm. The person who asks for options, receives ten properties that match exactly what they requested, and replies, “Do you have something else?” The buyer who is ready until it is time to decide, and then needs three more months to think. The one who disappeared after asking for a price came back after the price went up, and asked for the old price.

For a long time, these moments frustrated me. But they taught me that most people do not have a money problem. They have a decision problem. We are a generation that earns, spends, plans and postpones, often all at the same time.

You can earn a lot and still not be wealthy

One idea I keep returning to is that you can earn twenty million naira a year and still not be wealthy. Income is what comes in. Wealth is what stays and grows. Two people can earn the same salary and end up in completely different places ten years later, simply because one converted part of that income into assets and the other converted all of it into lifestyle.

Wealthy people do not always look wealthy. Some of the most financially secure people I have met do not drive the loudest cars. And some of the people who look the richest are one bad month away from panic.

So the question I now ask myself, and the people I speak with, is simple: what exactly are you converting your income into?

Real estate is bigger than land and a house

One conversation changed how I explain property to people. A Nigerian living in Canada called me after watching a video I had made about a commercial development in Ibadan. A few minutes in, he said something I have since heard from many people: “To me, real estate has always meant two things. You buy land and keep it, or you build a house to live in.”

That is how many of us were raised to think about property. Land is pride. A house is security. Both are good. But they are only part of the picture.

Some assets are for appreciation. Some assets are for cash flow. Land grows in value while you wait, but it does not pay you while you wait. A shop, a rental apartment or a short-let can pay you while it grows. When I explained this, the whole conversation changed. We stopped talking about a single plot and started talking about a plan.

Not long after, I had almost the same conversation with another Nigerian abroad. He had never considered property as something that could produce income. He liked what he heard. He even had a deposit ready. But he planned to buy more than a year later. I had to tell him honestly that the option he liked might not be there by then. The right asset rarely waits for our calendars.

Patience is not the same as understanding

Another lesson came from buyers who purchase property with a five-year plan and then become anxious when the value has not doubled in eight months.

I used to think the answer was simply to tell people to be patient. Now I think the real mistake is not impatience. It is entering an investment without knowing what you are waiting for. Is it a road under construction? A growing population? New businesses moving in? If you do not know what should drive the value, every month of waiting feels like a loss.

Don’t just trust. Verify

The hardest lesson is about trust. Many Nigerians abroad send money home and leave a relative to handle everything. The intention is love. But love is not a process. Money gets misused. Documents are not checked. Sites are not visited.

My advice is never to stop trusting family. It is to stop relying on trust alone. Have a lawyer who checks the title. Have a surveyor who confirms the land. Let family monitor. And yes, check the consultant too, including people like me. Professionals can be dishonest. Don’t just trust. Verify.

I would rather a client ask me ten uncomfortable questions before buying than discover after payment that there was something they should have checked. Closing a deal is good. Knowing that the person understood exactly what they were buying is better.

What I am building

When I started, I thought success in sales would be measured by how many properties I sold. I still care about that. But I care more now about something harder to count: whether the people I speak with make better decisions with their money because of the conversation we had.

I want to keep learning, keep growing and keep building something that means more than a sales record. And I will say it plainly, the way I sometimes say it to myself on difficult days: watch out for a few years when you hear my name.

Not because I will have sold the most land. But because I hope my name will stand for something many Nigerians are still searching for when it comes to money and property: honest guidance, good judgment and trust that is earned, not assumed. The mirror is still there. Every inspection, every delayed payment, every late-night call from abroad shows me something new. And the biggest thing it has shown me is that before people buy property, they need to understand their own relationship with money.

item.title: From “Behind The Scenes” to “Call of My Life”: 5 All-Time Highest-Grossing Nollywood Movies
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.description:
From Funke Akindele’s record-smashing "Behind The Scenes" and "A Tribe Called Judah" to Toyin Abraham’s "Oversabi Aunty" and the mid-year hit "Call of My Life," these five blockbusters redefined commercial success across Nigerian cinemas.

The post From “Behind The Scenes” to “Call of My Life”: 5 All-Time Highest-Grossing Nollywood Movies appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
Toyin Abraham’s directorial comedy drama Oversabi Aunty is now streaming on Netflix and Kava.

Nigerian cinema has witnessed an unprecedented commercial evolution over recent years, with local box office totals soaring past figures once considered unthinkable. From the era when a four-hundred-million-Naira milestone set the nationwide ceiling to an era defined by multi-billion-Naira theatrical runs, audiences across West Africa continue to show up in massive numbers for homegrown storytelling.

Here is a look at the five highest-grossing Nollywood blockbusters in history that have continually redefined theatrical success, shattered industry records, and set historic commercial benchmarks across Nigerian cinemas.

A Tribe Called Judah (2023) — Domestic Box Office: ₦1.40 Billion

When this family heist drama landed in Nigerian cinemas on 15 December 2023, few anticipated just how dramatically it would reset the financial ceiling for homegrown features. Directed by Funke Akindele and Tobi Makinde for the Funke Ayotunde Akindele Network (FAAN), the story follows Jedidah Judah—played by Akindele herself—and her five sons from different fathers as they scheme to rob a luxury furniture shop to fund their mother’s life-saving medical care. Supported by a stellar lineup including Timini Egbuson, Jide Kene Achufusi, Uzee Usman, Tobi Makinde, Olumide Oworu, Nse Ikpe Etim, and Genoveva Umeh, the narrative struck a deep chord across multiplexes.

By the end of its theatrical run, the project had earned over ₦1.40 Billion, making history as the very first Nollywood title to surpass the ₦1 Billion domestic milestone and cementing Funke Akindele’s status as a formidable box office power.

A Tribe Called Judah poster celebrating its historic ₦1 Billion box office milestone. Photo Credit: Filmone/Instagram

Everybody Loves Jenifa (2024) — Domestic Box Office: ₦1.88 Billion

FAAN Studios returned to the festive release window on 13 December 2024 with a comedy-drama co-directed by Funke Akindele and Tunde Olaoye. Centred on the enduring popularity of the lead character, the narrative charts Jenifa’s latest misadventures across global settings, societal expectations, and personal choices, bolstered by on-screen performances from Falz, Layi Wasabi, Patience Ozokwor, and Stan Nze.

Building rapidly on its festive debut, the feature went on to generate ₦1.88 Billion in local ticket sales. The milestone surpassed Akindele’s previous commercial record and established an extraordinary streak of back-to-back record-breaking theatrical hits.

Funke Akindele and Falz on the ₦1 Billion milestone poster for Everybody Loves Jenifa. Photo Credit: Funke Akindele/Instagram

Oversabi Aunty (2025) — Domestic Box Office: ₦1.17 Billion

Toyin Abraham made her big-screen directorial debut with this comedy-drama from Toyin Abraham Films, which opened in cinemas nationwide on 19 December 2025. The plot introduces Toun, an overzealous church usher and self-styled neighborhood moral authority whose relentless meddling in family and community affairs triggers widespread hilarity and domestic chaos. Abraham leads an ensemble cast alongside Mike Ezuruonye, Lateef Adedimeji, Mercy Aigbe, Odunlade Adekola, Femi Adebayo, and Efe Irele.

Finishing its run at ₦1.17 Billion, the project set a career-high theatrical record for Toyin Abraham, making her the second filmmaker in Nigerian cinema history to steer a feature past the ₦1 Billion threshold.

Toyin Abraham and cast members on the ₦1 Billion milestone poster for Oversabi Aunty. Photo Credit: Filmone/Instagram

Behind The Scenes (2025) — Domestic Box Office: ₦2.76 Billion

Arriving in cinemas on 12 December 2025, this festive satire from FAAN Studios, co-directed by Funke Akindele and Tunde Olaoye, takes an unfiltered look at the ambition and internal friction governing the film industry. The story centers on Aderonke Fernandez—portrayed by Scarlet Gomez—a wealthy real estate mogul whose generosity is continually exploited by her extended family until she decides enough is enough. Akindele stars alongside an expansive cast featuring Tobi Bakre, Uzor Arukwe, Uche Montana, Destiny Etiko, and Ini Dima-Okojie.

The release made immediate history by crossing half a billion Naira within twelve days, before going on to break every existing West African box office record. It became the first Nollywood movie to cross the ₦2 Billion barrier, topping all-time theatrical rankings with a total gross of ₦2.76 Billion.

Funke Akindele on the milestone poster for Behind The Scenes after crossing ₦2 Billion.

Call of My Life (2026) — Domestic Box Office: ₦902 Million

Directed by Dammy Twitch, written by Uzoamaka Power, and produced by Blessing Uzzi under Bluhouse Studios, this romantic comedy was released in cinemas on 15 May 2026. The story follows Soluchi, a heartbroken call-centre agent whose life takes a sharp turn when a routine customer call with a charming presenter named Eli rekindles her belief in love. The cast stars Uzoamaka Power alongside Andrew Yaw Bunting, Beverly Osu, Zubby Michael, Broda Shaggi, Nkem Owoh, and Patience Ozokwor.

The project completely redefined non-festive box office expectations by becoming the highest-grossing mid-year release outside the traditional December festive window. It crossed the ₦600 Million mark faster than any non-December release in Nollywood history, finishing its theatrical run at ₦902 Million and outperforming legacy blockbusters like Battle on Buka Street and Omo Ghetto: The Saga.

The stars of Call of My Life gather for the film’s Lagos premiere. Featured from left are Andrew Bunting, Uzoamaka Power, veteran actor Nkem Owoh, producer Blessing Uzzi, director Dammy Twitch, and actress Beverly Osu. Photo Credit: Uzoamaka Power/Instagram
